title: Daube de Boeuf Provençale
subtitle: Provençal beef braise with olives, orange, and red wine
excerpt: Beef braised slowly in red wine with olives, orange peel, and herbs until completely tender. A defining dish of Provence, and one that improves substantially when made a day ahead.
sourceNotes: The daube is the classic Provençal braise. Elizabeth David, A Book of Mediterranean Food (1950) and French Provincial Cooking (1960), devotes considerable attention to the daube, calling it 'one of the best dishes in the whole repertoire of Provençal cooking.' Richard Olney, Simple French Food (1974), gives a method close to this one. The daube traditionally marinates overnight before cooking; this version skips the marinade for a weekday-accessible approach.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze for up to 3 months. The flavour of a daube holds very well in the freezer. Thaw overnight and reheat gently.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The daube improves considerably if made a day ahead and reheated. The flavours deepen and the sauce thickens. Reheat gently on the hob or in the oven at 150°C for 25 minutes.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Provençal method of slow-braising meat in wine with aromatics and, typically, olives and orange peel. The word comes from the daubière, a sealed earthenware pot with a concave lid that held water or ice to prevent steam escaping. The daube is cooked low and slow, often 3 hours or more.

content.text: is Provençal braised beef. The sauce is built from red wine, tomatoes, olives, and a strip of dried orange peel, the last ingredient is the one that marks it as Provençal rather than any other regional braise. The beef cooks for three hours at a very low temperature until it falls apart, and the sauce around it becomes dark and deeply flavoured.
Make this dish a day ahead: the flavour on reheating is markedly better than on the day it is cooked.

content.text: Heat the oven to 150°C fan. Pat the beef dry and season well with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over high heat. Brown the beef in batches for 3 to 4 minutes per side until deeply coloured on all surfaces. Do not crowd the pan. Transfer to the Dutch oven as each batch is done.

In the same frying pan, fry the lardons over medium heat for 3 minutes. Add the onion and carrot and cook for 5 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute. Transfer to the Dutch oven.

Pour the wine into the frying pan and bring to the boil, scraping up the browned bits. Pour into the Dutch oven along with the tinned tomatoes. Add the olives, orange peel, thyme, and bay. Season. The liquid should come halfway up the beef; add a little water if needed.
Bring to a gentle simmer on the hob. Cover tightly, transfer to the oven, and cook at 150°C for 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours, until the beef is completely tender and falls apart when pressed.
Remove the thyme sprigs, bay, and orange peel. Taste and adjust seasoning. Serve with egg noodles, mashed potato, or crusty bread.

items.symptom: The beef is still tough after 3 hours
items.cause: The oven temperature was too low, or the beef chuck pieces were very large.
items.fix: Continue cooking for a further 30 minutes at 160°C. Chuck is a forgiving cut that only improves with longer cooking. Check the liquid level and add a splash of water if needed.

items.cause: Too much liquid was added, or the pot was not fully sealed.
items.fix: Remove the beef pieces and reduce the sauce on the hob over medium heat until it coats a spoon. Return the beef to the sauce.

items.cause: Brined or low-quality olives were used, and they cooked for the full 3 hours.
items.fix: Add the olives only in the final 30 minutes of cooking to preserve their flavour and prevent bitterness. Rinse brined olives before adding.

items.symptom: The orange flavour is too strong
items.cause: Too much peel was used, or the pith (white part) was included.
items.fix: For the next batch, use a single strip of peel with no pith. The orange should be a background note rather than a dominant flavour.

content.text: The daube belongs to the interior of Provence, the Var, the Vaucluse, and the lands around Arles. The sealed daubière traditionally sat in the embers of the fire all afternoon and evening, allowing the beef to cook in its own steam and the wine to reduce and concentrate around it. The orange peel is the most distinctly Provençal signature: it appears in no other regional braise in France and links the dish to the citrus orchards of the Midi. Elizabeth David described the finished sauce as 'that dark, oleaginous, shining juice which is one of the hallmarks of Provençal cooking.'
